newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish exporters, farmers welcome punt's fall.
newsitem.headline: Irish exporters, farmers welcome punt's fall.

text.p: Exporters and farmers on Thursday welcomed a sharp drop in the punt, noting that the Irish exporting sector would have sustained losses of 1.4 billion in a full-year if the punt's recent strength had been maintained.

Both groups have been lobbying the government over the exchange rate in recent weeks, arguing that a 10 percent appreciation of the Irish pound against the main ERM currencies since last summer has unfairly penalised Irish exports.

"We are very happy. This is what the whole purpose of our exercise was to achieve, what hopefully started yesterday in terms of an adjustment of the exchange rate of the punt," Con Lucey, chief economist at the Irish Farmers' Association (IFA), said.
Exporters also saw the sharp sell-off of the Irish pound, which hit a five-year low against sterling and plunged 6.5 pfennigs against the mark on Wednesday, as favourable.
Alan Fitzgibbon, senior economist at the Irish Trade Board, said the main issue it had had to deal with over the last year was Irish pound strength against the mark and other ERM currencies.

"We have been helping companies to deal with that, we have a task force going to help them and against that backdrop this movement, sudden as it seems to be, is not an unfavourable development for an export constituency," he told Reuters.

But IREX, an Irish exporters' group, noted that firms with a high level of dependence on imports were feeling the pinch and said they would prefer to have seen a gradual, orderly move in the punt rather than a sudden, sharp drop.

"We would much prefer if the change had been on a gradual, planned basis rather just unilateral withdrawal of support which has caused some problems for some companies," Frank Mulcahy, chief executive of IREX, told Reuters.
He said firms dependent on imports had found their costs had suddenly soared overnight.
"You can acclimatise to this in stages, over a period but when it is an overnight shock it does hit individual firms very heavily," Mulcahy said.
But for exporters, the drop in the punt was a good move which restored competitiveness which has been seriously eroded, Mulcahy said.
Farmers, who have seen three revaluations of the Irish green pound since November, are now hopeful that some of this could be reversed.
"If the punt falls further than its closing point yesterday, then very shortly after that the possibility of green pound devaluations start to trigger in," Lucey noted.

The revaluations have cut the value of CAP (Common Agricultural Policy) supports by 8.8 percent while the strength of the Irish pound means returns from France and Germany are down by about 10 percent, the IFA says.
The farming sector has also been struggling to come to terms with the BSE crisis in the beef industry which has seen cattle prices collapse by 20 to 25 percent over a two-year period.

"We hope that yesterday does mark the turning point of the situation and that we see, preferably a gradual, correction in the currency value," Lucey said, adding that the IFA would ideally like to see the punt back at its central ERM rate against the mark of 2.41.
